Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-28
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lina Chen (Redwood SE), Alex Morgan (DataForge ML Eng), Priya Nair (DataForge Platform Eng), Jordan Lee (CTO)
Recording: enabled

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Deep dive into repeat OOMs and intermittent CUDA errors observed during model serving; focus on retry semantics and timeout tuning.
- Discussed KV cache behavior with long prefix caching and batching trade-offs.
- Action: share benchmark sheet, reproduce on on-prem infra, collect driver/trace logs.

Topics:
- OOMs during peak bursts and long sequences
- Timeouts and end-to-end retry semantics (client, gateway, runtime)
- CUDA error patterns and driver mismatches
- KV cache cold/warm behavior and eviction interactions with batching
- Quantization impacts on memory and latency
- VPC / on-prem considerations for driver versions and GPU access

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick intros?
[00:07] Alex: Alex here, ML eng mostly on serving and infra monitoring. We've seen repeated OOMs during high burst windows, especially on 4k token requests.
[00:14] Priya: Priya, platform, I'm looking at the autoscaler and the node-level metrics.
[00:18] Jordan: Jordan here. We want to understand risk if we move larger workloads to Redwood Dedicated or try on-prem.
[00:25] Lina: Hi, Lina SE. I'll be digging into traces and kernel interactions.
[00:30] Samir: Cool. Quick agenda — Lina will walk through patterns, then we talk retry semantics and mitigation options, then next steps.

[00:48] Lina: So we looked at the crash logs you shared. Two main modes: big sequence OOMs where KV cache size plus activation memory spikes, and short burst OOMs tied to simultaneous batch scheduling.
[00:58] Alex: One detail: for the long sequences we do prefix caching — we call it kay-vee cache in our notes — sometimes the cache doesn't warm and we see big mem spikes. Could be a bug or just eviction thrashing.
[01:12] Lina: Right, eviction thrash sounds likely. When shards re-materialize the KV, memory momentarily doubles. Also quantization profile matters: we saw FP16 plus 4-bit quantization combos where memory layout is a bit odd and some kernels allocate temp buffers.
[01:28] Priya: We also observed some CUDA driver warnings a few hours before the OOMs, but not always. The errors sometimes read as "cooda peer timeout" in the logs — probably a transcription of c-o-o-d-a but I mean CUDA.
[01:40] Samir: That's expected; driver mismatches show as odd runtime behavior. Lina, can you summarize the typical stack trace lines we saw?
[01:47] Lina: Sure. Typically: runtime alloc fail -> cudaMalloc returned out of memory -> then a subsequent "device lost" on rare cases -> then retries from the gateway. The gateway's retry semantics are important: by default the client sees a 504 or 500 and then retries, which can make a thundering herd.
[02:06] Alex: That's a big concern. Our client side has retry-on-5xx enabled with exponential backoff but low jitter. In bursts that just amplifies the load.
[02:17] Samir: Ok mitigation split: client side and server side. Client: add full jitter and circuit breaker; Server: apply backpressure, prefixed queueing, and smarter scheduling to avoid starting new large batches when memory is near threshold.

[02:36] Priya: About timeouts — we have 30s gateway timeout and runtime times out at 45s. Sometimes the runtime is mid-generation and the gateway gives up and kills the connection; that leaves the runtime with a dangling worker until it notices.
[02:49] Lina: Right. We recommend aligning gateway and runtime timeouts so you don't get half-done work. Also, introduce cancel propagation so if gateway closes, runtime cancels promptly. We saw cases where the runtime didn't get the cancel due to network flap in VPC peering.
[03:04] Jordan: For on-prem, we care about driver versions — do you pin drivers? We've run into weird issues with 525 vs 535.
[03:12] Lina: We publish supported driver matrix but customers on-prem must match the supported driver + CUDA runtime versions. Mismatches can lead to subtle kernel fallbacks or increased memory use. We'll send the exact matrix.

[03:28] Samir: Let's talk KV cache and batching interactions — Alex you mentioned cold cache. Can you walk through a user request pattern?
[03:36] Alex: Sure. Typical user: interactive chat history plus a 2k token system prompt. On a cold start the KV cache has to be rebuilt and that causes extra memory and latency. If multiple requests for the same model happen, they can be coalesced but our app tends to burst concurrently.
[03:50] Lina: There are two levers: prefix caching (persistent across sessions) and transient per-request caching. Prefix caching reduces recompute but increases resident memory. If we tune eviction thresholds and shard the cache, we can reduce worst-case spikes.
[04:04] Priya: Do you recommend smaller shards? We hit cross-shard duplication once.
[04:08] Lina: Shard sizing is workload dependent. For chat-heavy workloads with long histories, larger shard size with LRU eviction works better. For highly concurrent short queries, smaller shards reduce duplication. We'll recommend a config after seeing your sample distribution.

[04:27] Alex: Quantization — we tested 4-bit with some models; latency looked fine but OOMs increased. Is that expected?
[04:34] Lina: Sometimes. 4-bit quantization reduces parameter memory but depending on the kernel it increases temporary workspace (for dequant/reshuffle). Also, mixed precision plus 4-bit code paths can allocate extra buffers. If quantization is aggressive, you might need to increase workspace limits or prefer grouped quantization kernels that are more memory efficient.
[04:52] Samir: Practical mitigation list — 1) apply client jitter + circuit breaking, 2) align timeouts and enable cancel propagation, 3) tune KV cache shard/eviction, 4) pick quantization profile + kernel combo we've validated.

[05:10] Priya: About retries — we saw retries from both client and the Redwood gateway. How do you recommend coordinating?
[05:16] Lina: Gateway has exponential backoff and a retry budget. For platform you can lower gateway retries for long-running requests and let client-side be more conservative. Also, add idempotency tokens to avoid double compute on non-idempotent flows.
[05:30] Alex: We're also seeing a pattern where a single worker OOMs, gets restarted, and the scheduler reassigns a heavy request to another busy worker, causing cascading failures.
[05:39] Lina: That's cascade. One fix: soft-preemption — when a worker nears memory threshold, it refuses new large batches and the scheduler prefers cold-start workers with headroom. Also, use backfill limits so you don't overload fewer GPUs.

[05:58] Jordan: For on-prem tests, we want to reproduce OOMs. What logs/metrics do you need?
[06:03] Lina: Driver versions, cuda runtime, per-worker memory footprint (rss + GPU alloc), batch sizes, exact prompt lengths, and the ctx sequence distributions. Also the GPU dmesg if the device kernel logged anything.
[06:16] Samir: We'll send a template for logs and an example benchmark sheet. Alex — can you add estimated token distributions to that sheet?
[06:24] Alex: Yep, I'll add.

[06:28] Priya: One more note: we have strict VPC peering and private on-prem nodes behind NAT. Can that affect timeout/cancel propagation?
[06:36] Lina: Yes, network flaps and NAT timeouts can delay cancel signals. For on-prem we recommend colocating the control-plane agent with the runtime or using a dedicated management network so cancels are low latency.

[06:49] Samir: Let's capture a quick runbook if OOMs happen in production — Lina?
[06:53] Lina: Runbook (short): 1) identify offending worker and its memory trend, 2) check recent kernel allocations and temp workspace spikes, 3) look for heavy quantization or model variant mis-match, 4) if cascade detected, throttle ingress and enable circuit breaker, 5) collect traces and escalate to SE. We'll attach a longer doc.

[07:14] Alex: There were also intermittent 'cuMemAlloc' error codes that looked like driver bug. Any mitigation besides driver update?
[07:21] Lina: Only real fix is driver/runtime alignment or changing kernels that avoid the buggy path. We can also soft-fail requests earlier with a preflight memory check to avoid hitting the kernel error.

[07:34] Priya: Anything about monitoring? We need threshold alerts that are not too noisy.
[07:38] Samir: Use a two-tier alert: soft-warning at 70% GPU memory with sustained 30s, hard alert at 90% or OOMs. Also alert on increased retry rates and rising lat p99.

[07:51] Jordan: Can you share sample configs for caching and shard sizing?
[07:55] Lina: Yes, we'll share a config repo snippet. Also a note — some names in logs may be mis-attr but we'll annotate the spreadsheet.

[08:06] (Silence while Samir types)
[08:11] Samir: Recap: we'll share benchmark spreadsheet + driver matrix + runbook. Lina will run targeted repro on a small cluster and share traces. DataForge will provide sample prompt distributions and open window for on-prem testing week of 2026-04-06.
[08:27] Alex: Sounds good. Also please include guidance on retry budgets and recommended client jitter values.
[08:33] Samir: Will do. Anything else?
[08:36] Priya: Could we get an ATO-ish doc for audit and security for on-prem? Need to show our infosec team.
[08:42] Samir: Yes, we'll share the security checklist and SOC2 references; note there may be redacted items for hosted but on-prem doc has full details.

[08:52] Jordan: Thanks, that helps.

[08:54] Samir: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the sheet and proposed dates.

[09:00] Meeting end.
